title: Home to the hills
hook: after battles with Mughal forces, Guru Hargobind settles at Kiratpur and spends his last years quietly

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloak with fifty-two tassels, and the prisoners who walked out holding on. Your line was no one freed alone. Did you hand someone their tassel? Day sixty-eight.

Some people never learn to stop. The firefighter who can't sit through dinner without listening for the siren. The parent who, years after the kids leave, still sleeps with one ear open. The soldier who comes home and can't find the off switch. Guru Hargobind had spent most of his life on guard. A boy Guru after his father's killing. Two swords. An army. A prison fort. And then, in his later years, real battles. Today we follow him out of the fighting and up into the foothills, where the sixth Guru did something his whole life had not trained him for. He rested.
screen: `PEOPLE WHO NEVER STOP.` → `A LIFE ON GUARD.` → `THEN, THE FOOTHILLS.`

segments.voice: In the years around 1634, the peace between the Guru and the Mughal authorities broke down. Tradition tells of several clashes. One began, the story goes, with a dispute over a hunting hawk. The accounts list four battles, in and around Amritsar and further south, and in each the Guru's small force held its own against much larger ones. Sikhs remember these as the first battles fought by a Guru, and the year a Sikh boy named Tyag Mal fought so hard he earned a new name; that's a story for day seventy-four. But the Guru did not want endless war. After the last battle, at Kartarpur near the Beas river, he led his family and followers north, into the Shivalik foothills, to a town on the Sutlej river called Kiratpur. Kiratpur had been founded by his son, Baba Gurditta, on land given by a hill raja. It was quiet, green, out of the way. And there, for about his last ten years, Guru Hargobind lived peacefully. He kept horses and a hunting ground, but the fighting was over. He preached, received visitors, looked after his community, and prepared the next Guru. He passed over his sons and chose a grandson, Har Rai, a gentle boy of about fourteen. Guru Hargobind died at Kiratpur in 1644. Here's what the story teaches: the same Guru who first wore two swords knew when to put them down. Miri piri was never about fighting forever. It was about holding strength and stillness in the right balance, and in the end the balance tipped toward rest.
screen: `BATTLES AROUND 1634.` · `NORTH TO KIRATPUR.` · `TEN QUIET YEARS.` · `A GENTLE GRANDSON CHOSEN.` · then, large: `EVEN WARRIORS REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest after a hard week. Let this be the easiest sit of the week. Lean back if you can. Let your jaw loosen, your hands go heavy, your shoulders come down from your ears. Think of what you've carried these last few days, and set each piece down, one at a time, like a weapon laid on a table. You don't have to fix anything. Nothing is guarding the gate right now. Just rest. The bell holds the time.
Home to the hills. After years of conflict, Guru Hargobind settled at Kiratpur in the foothills and spent his last years in peace.
Your line: even warriors rest. Today, take one real rest on purpose: a nap, a slow walk, an evening with the phone in another room. Day sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, where Guru Hargobind spent his last years, is a place of Sikh pilgrimage, and many Sikh families today take the ashes of their loved ones there to be scattered in the river.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Kiratpur, the town on the Sutlej; kirat can mean praise.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old soldier retires.
what it means: the Guru who first wore two swords knew when to put them down, and chose a gentle successor.
what a scholar hears: Kiratpur was founded by Baba Gurditta in the 1620s; Guru Hargobind died there in 1644, choosing his grandson Har Rai.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Hargobind's battles (c. 1634–1635) and his last years at Kiratpur

notes: The four battles (Amritsar, Lahira/Mehraj, Kartarpur and one more, c. 1628–1635) are counted and dated differently by historians; kept general. Confirm.
The hawk dispute (Shah Jahan's hawk taken by Sikhs) is tradition; confirm.
'About his last ten years' at Kiratpur (c. 1635–1644); confirm. Kiratpur founded by Baba Gurditta c. 1626 on land from the Raja of Kahlur; confirm.
Har Rai's age at succession given as about fourteen (born 1630). Confirm.
howItsDone: the custom of scattering ashes at Kiratpur Sahib (Patalpuri); confirm.
